title: India's Chip Sector Hits $1.4 Billion in Funding as Dholera Fab Races Toward 2027
excerpt: A Tracxn report timed to SEMICON India 2026 shows funding up 10x since 2021 — but services and design still dominate, and no approved fab is in commercial production yet.
body:
• A new Tracxn report shows India's semiconductor sector has drawn $1.4 billion in cumulative all-time equity funding across 281 companies, with nearly half — $701 million — raised since 2025 alone.
  • Annual funding has climbed from $49 million in 2021 to $473 million in 2025, a five-year compound growth rate above 36%, with Bengaluru capturing 40% of all equity funding.
  • Top funded names include Tessolve Semiconductor ($213 million), ILJIN Electronics ($198 million) and VVDN ($129 million), but the sector remains dominated by services and design rather than manufacturing.
  • The report lands days before SEMICON India 2026 opens September 17 in New Delhi, with the Tata-PSMC fab in Dholera targeting India's first domestically produced chips around mid-2027.

India's chip ambitions are finally drawing serious money. A new Tracxn report published ahead of SEMICON India 2026 shows the country's semiconductor sector has attracted $1.4 billion in cumulative all-time equity funding across 281 companies — with nearly half of that total, $701 million, raised since 2025.

The data, reported by the Times of India, captures an industry accelerating from a standing start. Annual funding rose from $49 million in 2021 to $473 million in 2025, a five-year compound annual growth rate above 36%. In 2026 alone, $228 million has already been raised — roughly on pace with last year's total.

Where the money goes

India now hosts 3,557 semiconductor-related companies, though only 281 have secured funding and 142 have raised equity, according to Tracxn. The top cumulative fundraisers are Tessolve Semiconductor at $213 million, ILJIN Electronics at $198 million and VVDN at $129 million.

Since 2025, the best-funded business models have been electronic manufacturing services ($313 million), embedded hardware ($51.9 million), power management integrated circuits and fabless semiconductor makers. Geographically, Bengaluru dominates: the city accounts for about 626 companies and a full 40.1% of all equity funding, followed by Noida (16.4%), Gurugram (10.7%), Kochi (8.8%) and Hyderabad (6.2%).

Design-heavy, manufacturing-light

The honest picture is more nuanced than the headline number. As TechObserver.in notes, the sector "remains dominated by services and design rather than manufacturing," and none of the government-approved fabs have commenced commercial production yet.

The manufacturing side is where the real test lies. The India Semiconductor Mission — notified in December 2021 with a ₹76,000 crore outlay — has approved about ten projects worth ₹1.6 lakh crore in total investment. The flagship is the Tata Electronics-PSMC fab in Dholera, Gujarat (₹91,000 crore, 50,000 wafer starts a month), with construction about half complete as of April and first production targeted for mid-2027. But TechTimes reported in July that the fab may open production at 90nm rather than the promised 28nm node, and Gartner analyst Kanishka Chauhan has flagged rare-earth supply disruptions as a risk.

Progress is real elsewhere: Micron's assembly and test plant in Sanand shipped its first DRAM and NAND modules after a February inauguration, Kaynes Semicon's OSAT unit has been operational since March, and CG Semi's pilot line is expected to produce the first "Made-in-India" chip. The Union Cabinet approved ISM 2.0 in July — ₹1.27 lakh crore over 12 years — with IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw saying "all the first four units that got approved are going to complete their pilot line within this year. Fab will take time."

"The pace of construction in Dholera is rapid, and Tata Electronics is making real progress in bringing the chip fab to life."

— Kanishka Chauhan, senior principal analyst, Gartner

The exit problem

One number should temper the excitement: acquisitions remain the primary exit route, with 62 acquisitions against 42 IPOs, and an average of 11.8 years from first funding to acquisition. The largest exits — eInfochips ($282 million), Narayan Powertech ($262 million), SmartPlay Technologies ($180 million) — are all acquisitions. Recent listings like Tempsens Instruments (IPO in August 2026, $263 million market cap) and Merritronix are exceptions in an ecosystem that still sells rather than lists.

What to watch

The immediate stage is SEMICON India 2026, opening September 17 at Yashobhoomi in Dwarka, New Delhi — the fifth edition, to be inaugurated by Prime Minister Narendra Modi with global industry leaders, state governments and experts in attendance. The longer questions: whether 2026 funding can match 2025's $473 million pace, how ISM 2.0 draws fresh fab and design investment, and — the big one — whether mid-2027 brings India's first genuinely domestically fabricated chip. The money is flowing. Manufacturing has to follow.
